fr:title.text: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Soundness Regimes and the Proximity-Gap Conjectures

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The same protocol has different soundness depending on how far from the code you are willing to reason, and the parameters used in production sit in the regime where the analysis is conjectural. This page is the reason list decoding is in this corpus at all.

fr:title.text: Low-Degree Testing, from FRI to WHIR

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Low-Degree Testing, from FRI to WHIR

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The heart of the transparent stack. The lineage is short and each step answers one specific complaint: FRI tests proximity to a Reed–Solomon code by folding, STIR attacks its query cost at constant rate, and WHIR attacks STIR's verification cost while joining the univariate and multilinear worlds.

These pages should be the most careful in the corpus. The soundness statements are where the regimes matter, where the deployed parameters are conjectural, and where ArkLib's hardest formalisation work sits.
Fast Reed–Solomon Interactive Oracle Proof of Proximity. The protocol most of the deployed proving stack rests on, and the one every construction later in this section is a response to.

Questions this page should answer:
The folding map: halving the degree by splitting into even and odd parts and taking a random combination. Why the folded word is a codeword when the original is.
Commit phase and query phase; the round-consistency check the verifier performs.
Parameters and their interaction: rate, folding factor, number of rounds, number of query repetitions.
Prover cost — encoding, Merkle hashing, and where the time actually goes.
The soundness statement, with the regime named explicitly.
What ArkLib's ProofSystem/Fri states, and how far the proof gets.
Reading: Ben-Sasson, Bentov, Horesh, and Riabzev, Fast Reed–Solomon Interactive Oracle Proofs of Proximity (ICALP 2018); the SoK for the corrected attributions.

fr:title.text: Poseidon, and Why Ethereum Walked Away

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Poseidon, and Why Ethereum Walked Away

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Poseidon (Grassi, Khovratovich, Rechberger, Roy, and Schofnegger, 2019) is a sponge over a prime field rather than over bits. Its permutation follows the HADES strategy: a few full rounds, where an S-box — typically x \mapsto x^5 — is applied to every element, and many partial rounds applying it to one, with an MDS matrix mixing the state between them. Poseidon2 later reworked the linear layer for speed. Because the whole function is field arithmetic, its cost inside a prime-field circuit is counted in multiplications, and it beat SHA-256 there by orders of magnitude.

The objection was always that the same algebraic structure that makes it cheap to arithmetise is what algebraic cryptanalysis attacks, and that parameters are generated per field and per state width rather than fixed once and studied for decades. The Ethereum Foundation took this seriously enough to fund the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative, with bounties up to $1 million scheduled to run through December 2026.

It was paused on 1 August 2026, and on 13 August Justin Drake announced that the Foundation is abandoning Poseidon for L1 in favour of SHA or BLAKE, calling it "an epic 8-year, 8-figure rabbit hole in post-quantum cryptography" reaching "its dream conclusion." His diagnosis is the memorable part: "In hindsight the key was not SNARK-friendly hashes, but hash-friendly SNARKs."

What changed is the proving side. Binius moved the arithmetic into towers of binary fields, where a Boolean computation costs what it should instead of paying to embed single bits into a large prime field. Flock (eprint 2026/1329) took that further for the specific shape of the problem — large batches of the same Boolean circuit — and reports 82k BLAKE3 compressions, 42k SHA-256 compressions, and 30k Keccak permutations per second on one core of an M4 Max, more than 660k BLAKE3 compressions per second on ten, over 9 times faster than Binius64 on SHA-256 and more than 500 times faster than the fastest elliptic-curve SNARK it measured against. Drake's figure for the resulting designs is roughly one million conventional hash calls per second on a laptop, at about 100 times the cost of native execution.

Poseidon was not broken, and nothing here says it will be. An engineering decision was reversed because a different part of the stack improved, which is worth separating clearly from a cryptanalytic result — the security argument never changed, only what it had to buy. The stated roadmap puts a production-grade leanVM in 2027 and consensus, data, and execution layer deployment in 2028.
Sources: Drake's announcement, Flock and its implementation, the Poseidon Cryptanalysis Initiative.

fr:title.text: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What a Verified zkVM Would Mean

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The statement at the top of the whole effort, written out honestly: which theorems compose, and which links in the chain are assumptions rather than proofs. It is the claim the whole effort will be judged on, and its general form is the issue of incorrect specification: a machine-checked proof is only ever as good as the statement it proves.

Questions this page should answer:
The chain: ISA specification, constraint system, arithmetisation soundness, IOP soundness, commitment security, Fiat–Shamir, recursion, extracted implementation.
Which links are proved today, which are stated, and which are not formalised at all.
The irreducible assumptions: hash security, conjectured proximity bounds, the compiler, the hardware.
Whether "verified" should mean the composed end-to-end theorem, or a set of component theorems with audited seams.
The 2027 target the project set, and what would have to be true for it to be met.
Sources: verified-zkevm.org, Verified-zkEVM overview.
